items.prompt: What is x XOR x for any fixed-width bit pattern x?

feedback.reason: At each position, a bit XOR itself is zero, so the entire fixed-width pattern cancels.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

XOR combines corresponding bits independently. Its one-bit table gives 0 XOR 0 = 0 and 1 XOR 1 = 0, so every position in x XOR x becomes zero. For example, 1011 XOR 1011 = 0000. Fixed width ensures both operands expose the same positions; the argument uses equality of patterns, not their numeric sign.

feedback.reason: Zero is the identity element for XOR.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

At one bit, 0 XOR 0 = 0 and 1 XOR 0 = 1. Applying that identity independently to every position leaves the complete pattern unchanged: 1011 XOR 0000 = 1011. This is why an XOR reduction can initialize its accumulator to zero without affecting later inputs.

items.prompt: Why can XOR operands be reordered when proving pair cancellation?

options.text: Fixed width forces one evaluation order.

feedback.reason: Reordering and regrouping bring equal values next to each other conceptually.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Commutativity gives a XOR b = b XOR a, and associativity gives (a XOR b) XOR c = a XOR (b XOR c). Therefore a sequence such as a XOR b XOR a can be reasoned about as (a XOR a) XOR b = 0 XOR b = b without physically sorting the input. Regrouping is a proof step enabled by these identities.

items.prompt: Every array value appears exactly twice except one value that appears once. What does XOR of all values produce?

options.text: The arithmetic sum of all values.

feedback.reason: Every duplicated bit pattern cancels with its equal partner.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Start with accumulator 0 and XOR every value. Associativity and commutativity let the proof group each duplicate pair as v XOR v = 0; each resulting zero disappears because x XOR 0 = x. After all pairs cancel, the one value with no partner is the only pattern left in the accumulator.

items.prompt: What is the XOR reduction of an empty sequence when the accumulator starts at zero?

feedback.reason: Zero is the neutral element for XOR reduction.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

A reduction needs an identity value that does not alter any input; for XOR that value is zero because x XOR 0 = x. With no sequence elements, the update step runs zero times, so the accumulator retains its initialized value 0. The result is defined by this explicit reduction contract rather than by guessing a special case.

items.prompt: A value appears three times and every other value appears twice. What remains after XOR reduction?

feedback.reason: XOR preserves whether each identical pattern occurs an odd or even number of times.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Three equal copies regroup as (x XOR x) XOR x = 0 XOR x = x. Every other value has even multiplicity and can be partitioned into equal pairs that reduce to zero. XOR therefore preserves only the odd/even parity of identical-pattern occurrences; it does not return the count three.

items.prompt: What is 5 XOR 3 in binary arithmetic?

feedback.reason: 0101 XOR 0011 equals 0110 because XOR sets only positions whose input bits differ.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Write both values at the same width: 5 = 0101 and 3 = 0011. From left to right the pairs are 0/0→0, 1/0→1, 0/1→1 and 1/1→0, producing 0110, which is 6. XOR sets a result bit exactly when the two input bits differ and never propagates a carry.

items.prompt: Can equal negative integers cancel under fixed-width two's-complement XOR?

options.text: Yes. Equal negative integers have identical fixed-width bit patterns, and x XOR x is zero.
No. Sign bits can never cancel.
XOR cancellation works only for positive values.
The operands must be reinterpreted as unsigned numeric values first.

feedback.reason: Self-cancellation depends on equality of bit patterns, not on numeric sign.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

A fixed-width two's-complement integer is stored as a bit pattern including its sign bit. Equal negative integers have identical patterns, and each corresponding pair is either 0 XOR 0 or 1 XOR 1, both zero. For example, in eight bits -1 is 11111111, and XORing it with itself yields 00000000.

items.prompt: Which multiplicity contract is required for the basic one-unique XOR solution?

options.text: Every non-answer value occurs an even canceling number of times, typically exactly twice, and the answer occurs an odd number of times.
Every value may occur any number of times with no further structure.

feedback.reason: The algorithm isolates one odd-frequency pattern only under a matching multiplicity guarantee.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Every even number of identical values can be grouped into pairs and canceled. If exactly one value has odd multiplicity, all but one of its copies also pair off, leaving that value alone. With two odd-frequency values a and b, the accumulator instead stores a XOR b, which generally identifies neither one; therefore the multiplicity promise is part of correctness.

items.prompt: Exactly two values appear once and every other value appears twice. What does XOR of all values produce?

options.text: The XOR of the two unique values, not either value individually.

feedback.reason: Paired values cancel, leaving a XOR b.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Every duplicated value cancels, so only the two singletons contribute: result = a XOR b. Because a and b are different, this result has at least one set bit marking a position where they differ. The aggregate alone is not either singleton; recovering both requires using such a bit to partition inputs and perform separate cancellations.

items.prompt: What does XOR reduction track for each bit position across a sequence?

options.text: Whether that bit is set in an odd number of inputs.
The exact number of set occurrences.
Whether the bit is set in at least one input.

feedback.reason: Each occurrence of a one toggles the accumulator bit.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

At one fixed position, each input one toggles the accumulator between zero and one, while an input zero leaves it unchanged. Two toggles cancel, so an even count ends at zero and an odd count ends at one. Positions are processed independently, which means the result preserves parity per bit but neither exact counts nor which input supplied each one.

items.prompt: Which XOR identities are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: x XOR y = y XOR x.

feedback.reason: XOR forms a cancellation algebra with zero identity.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The one-bit truth table proves x XOR x = 0 and x XOR 0 = x position by position. Swapping operands does not change whether their bits differ, so XOR is commutative. It is not idempotent: applying x twice cancels it, whereas an idempotent operation such as OR would preserve x.

items.prompt: Which problem contracts can be solved directly by one XOR reduction? Select all that apply.

options.text: One value occurs once and every other value occurs exactly twice.
Exactly one value has odd multiplicity and every other value has even multiplicity.
Determine whether XOR parity across all fixed-width values is zero.
Return every value with arbitrary nonzero frequency.

feedback.reason: Direct XOR reduction solves contracts expressible as one parity aggregate.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

One accumulator preserves only per-bit parity. It directly isolates one odd-frequency pattern when all others are even, and it can test whether the overall XOR parity is zero. It cannot list an arbitrary set of nonzero-frequency values because many different multisets collapse to the same aggregate and the missing identities cannot be reconstructed.

items.prompt: Which statements describe limitations of XOR cancellation? Select all that apply.

options.text: It loses exact multiplicity beyond even versus odd.
Two uncancelled values remain combined as their XOR.
It cannot generally replace arithmetic addition.

feedback.reason: XOR is powerful when the contract matches parity cancellation, but it is not a general multiset summary.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

XOR reduces each position to odd or even parity, so it discards exact counts. Two singletons survive only as a XOR b, and absence of carries means the aggregate is not an arithmetic sum. Sorting is unnecessary because XOR is associative and commutative. The technique is valid only when the requested answer can be recovered from this deliberately lossy parity summary.

items.prompt: Which statements about per-bit parity are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An odd number of one bits at a position produces one in the XOR result.
An even number of one bits at a position produces zero.
Each bit position is combined independently.
The result reveals the exact number of ones at each position.

feedback.reason: XOR is independent parity addition modulo two at every position.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

At each position, XOR is addition modulo two: an odd count of ones leaves one and an even count leaves zero. No carry moves information between positions, so they remain independent. Because counts one and three produce the same parity, the result cannot reveal the exact number of ones.

items.prompt: Arrange the algorithm for finding one odd-frequency value when every other value has even frequency.

elements.text: XOR every input value into the accumulator.
Use associativity and self-cancellation to eliminate even-frequency values.

feedback.reason: The implementation is a linear reduction, while the proof conceptually regroups equal values.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Initialize the accumulator with zero because x XOR 0 = x. Process each input exactly once with accumulator = accumulator XOR value. After the pass, use associativity and commutativity to regroup equal values in the proof: even-frequency groups cancel, and the promised single odd-frequency value remains. No physical sorting is performed.

items: Set accumulator = 0, XOR's identity.
For each input value, update accumulator = accumulator XOR value.
After the pass, invoke the multiplicity contract: every even-frequency pattern has canceled.
Return the accumulator, which equals the one promised odd-frequency value.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The proof groups equal values only conceptually; the implementation can process the input in any order because XOR is associative and commutative.

items.prompt: A fixed-width array of n values is reduced with XOR to find one odd-frequency value. Select time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: Each XOR operates on one fixed machine word.

feedback.reason: The reduction processes each input once.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The loop performs one fixed-width XOR for each of n values, so time is n·O(1) = O(n). It retains only the current accumulator and loop cursor, both fixed-width scalars, so auxiliary space is O(1). The input may be streamed because future values need no stored history.

items.prompt: An array contains n arbitrary-precision values, each represented with at most w bits. XORing two values costs O(w). Select total time and accumulator space.
constraints: The result accumulator also occupies O(w) bits.

feedback.reason: The fixed-word O(1) operation model does not apply when width grows with input.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

For arbitrary-precision values, one XOR may inspect up to w represented bits rather than acting as one machine-word primitive. Across n inputs, total time is n·O(w) = O(nw). The running aggregate must retain up to w bits, so accumulator space is O(w); this is the representation boundary behind the result.
